> ## Documentation Index
> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt
> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.

# Common workflows

> Step-by-step guides for exploring codebases, fixing bugs, refactoring, testing, and other everyday tasks with Claude Code.

This page collects short recipes for everyday development. For higher-level guidance on prompting and context management, see [Best practices](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices.md).

This page covers:

* [Prompt recipes](#prompt-recipes) for exploring code, fixing bugs, refactoring, testing, PRs, and documentation
* [Resume previous conversations](#resume-previous-conversations) so a task can span multiple sittings
* [Run parallel sessions with worktrees](#run-parallel-sessions-with-worktrees) so concurrent edits don't collide
* [Plan before editing](#plan-before-editing) to review changes before they touch disk
* [Delegate research to subagents](#delegate-research-to-subagents) to keep your main context clean
* [Pipe Claude into scripts](#pipe-claude-into-scripts) for CI and batch processing

## Prompt recipes

These are prompt patterns for everyday tasks like exploring unfamiliar code, debugging, refactoring, writing tests, and creating PRs. Each works in any Claude Code surface; adapt the wording to your project.

### Understand new codebases

For configuring Claude Code in a monorepo or large codebase, see [Monorepos and large repos](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/large-codebases.md).

#### Get a quick codebase overview

Suppose you've just joined a new project and need to understand its structure quickly.

**1. Navigate to the project root directory**

```bash theme={null}
cd /path/to/project 
```

Replace `/path/to/project` with the path to your project.

**2. Start Claude Code**

```bash theme={null}
claude 
```

**3. Ask for a high-level overview**

```text wrap theme={null}
give me an overview of this codebase
```

**4. Dive deeper into specific components**

```text wrap theme={null}
explain the main architecture patterns used here
```

```text wrap theme={null}
what are the key data models?
```

```text wrap theme={null}
how is authentication handled?
```

> [!TIP]
>
> Tips:
>
> * Start with broad questions, then narrow down to specific areas
> * Ask about coding conventions and patterns used in the project
> * Request a glossary of project-specific terms

#### Find relevant code

Suppose you need to locate code related to a specific feature or functionality.

**1. Ask Claude to find relevant files**

```text wrap theme={null}
find the files that handle user authentication
```

**2. Get context on how components interact**

```text wrap theme={null}
how do these authentication files work together?
```

**3. Understand the execution flow**

```text wrap theme={null}
trace the login process from front-end to database
```

> [!TIP]
>
> Tips:
>
> * Be specific about what you're looking for
> * Use domain language from the project
> * Install a [code intelligence plugin](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/code-intelligence.md) for your language to give Claude precise "go to definition" and "find references" navigation

***

### Fix bugs efficiently

Suppose you've encountered an error message and need to find and fix its source.

**1. Share the error with Claude**

```text wrap theme={null}
I'm seeing an error when I run npm test
```

**2. Ask for fix recommendations**

```text wrap theme={null}
suggest a few ways to fix the @ts-ignore in user.ts
```

**3. Apply the fix**

```text wrap theme={null}
update user.ts to add the null check you suggested
```

> [!TIP]
>
> Tips:
>
> * Tell Claude the command to reproduce the issue and get a stack trace
> * Mention any steps to reproduce the error
> * Let Claude know if the error is intermittent or consistent

***

### Refactor code

Suppose you need to update old code to use modern patterns and practices.

For porting an entire codebase to a new language, see [how Anthropic runs large-scale code migrations with Claude Code](https://claude.com/blog/ai-code-migration) on the blog.

**1. Identify legacy code for refactoring**

```text wrap theme={null}
find deprecated API usage in our codebase
```

**2. Get refactoring recommendations**

```text wrap theme={null}
suggest how to refactor utils.js to use modern JavaScript features
```

**3. Apply the changes safely**

```text wrap theme={null}
refactor utils.js to use ES2024 features while maintaining the same behavior
```

**4. Verify the refactoring**

```text wrap theme={null}
run tests for the refactored code
```

> [!TIP]
>
> Tips:
>
> * Ask Claude to explain the benefits of the modern approach
> * Request that changes maintain backward compatibility when needed
> * Do refactoring in small, testable increments

***

### Work with tests

Suppose you need to add tests for uncovered code.

**1. Identify untested code**

```text wrap theme={null}
find functions in NotificationsService.swift that are not covered by tests
```

**2. Generate test scaffolding**

```text wrap theme={null}
add tests for the notification service
```

**3. Add meaningful test cases**

```text wrap theme={null}
add test cases for edge conditions in the notification service
```

**4. Run and verify tests**

```text wrap theme={null}
run the new tests and fix any failures
```

Claude can generate tests that follow your project's existing patterns and conventions. When asking for tests, be specific about what behavior you want to verify. Claude examines your existing test files to match the style, frameworks, and assertion patterns already in use.

To improve coverage, ask Claude to identify edge cases you might have missed. Claude can analyze your code paths and suggest tests for error conditions, boundary values, and unexpected inputs that are often overlooked.

***

### Create pull requests

You can create pull requests by asking Claude directly ("create a pr for my changes"), or guide Claude through it step-by-step:

**1. Summarize your changes**

```text wrap theme={null}
summarize the changes I've made to the authentication module
```

**2. Generate a pull request**

```text wrap theme={null}
create a pr
```

**3. Review and refine**

```text wrap theme={null}
enhance the PR description with more context about the security improvements
```

To find the session later, run `claude --from-pr 1234` with your own PR number, which opens the session picker filtered to sessions linked to that PR, or paste the PR URL into the [`/resume` picker](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions#use-the-session-picker) search. Claude Code links the session to the PR when Claude creates it with `gh pr create` or `glab mr create`, and when Claude [works on an existing PR](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-view.md#pull-request-status).

> [!TIP]
>
> Review Claude's generated PR before submitting and ask Claude to highlight potential risks or considerations.

### Handle documentation

Suppose you need to add or update documentation for your code.

**1. Identify undocumented code**

```text wrap theme={null}
find functions without proper JSDoc comments in the auth module
```

**2. Generate documentation**

```text wrap theme={null}
add JSDoc comments to the undocumented functions in auth.js
```

**3. Review and enhance**

```text wrap theme={null}
improve the generated documentation with more context and examples
```

**4. Verify documentation**

```text wrap theme={null}
check if the documentation follows our project standards
```

> [!TIP]
>
> Tips:
>
> * Specify the documentation style you want (JSDoc, docstrings, etc.)
> * Ask for examples in the documentation
> * Request documentation for public APIs, interfaces, and complex logic

***

### Work in notes and non-code folders

Claude Code works in any directory. Run it inside a notes vault, a documentation folder, or any collection of markdown files to search, edit, and reorganize content the same way you would code.

The `.claude/` directory and `CLAUDE.md` sit alongside other tools' config directories without conflict. Claude reads files fresh on each tool call, so it sees edits you make in another application the next time it reads that file.

***

### Work with images

Suppose you need to work with images in your codebase, and you want Claude's help analyzing image content.

**1. Add an image to the conversation**

You can use any of these methods:

1. Drag and drop an image into the Claude Code window
2. Copy an image and paste it into the CLI with `Ctrl+V`, or with [`Alt+V` on Windows and WSL](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/interactive-mode#general-controls)
3. Provide an image path to Claude, for example "Analyze this image: /path/to/your/image.png"

**2. Ask Claude to analyze the image**

```text wrap theme={null}
What does this image show?
```

```text wrap theme={null}
Describe the UI elements in this screenshot
```

```text wrap theme={null}
Are there any problematic elements in this diagram?
```

**3. Use images for context**

```text wrap theme={null}
Here's a screenshot of the error. What's causing it?
```

```text wrap theme={null}
This is our current database schema. How should we modify it for the new feature?
```

**4. Get code suggestions from visual content**

```text wrap theme={null}
Generate CSS to match this design mockup
```

```text wrap theme={null}
What HTML structure would recreate this component?
```

> [!TIP]
>
> Tips:
>
> * Use images when text descriptions would be unclear or cumbersome
> * Include screenshots of errors, UI designs, or diagrams for better context
> * You can work with multiple images in a conversation
> * Image analysis works with diagrams, screenshots, mockups, and more
> * When Claude references images (for example, `[Image #1]`), `Cmd+Click` (Mac) or `Ctrl+Click` (Windows/Linux) the link to open the image in your default viewer

***

### Reference files and directories

Use @ to quickly include files or directories without waiting for Claude to read them.

**1. Reference a single file**

```text wrap theme={null}
Explain the logic in @src/utils/auth.js
```

This includes the content of the file in the conversation when it fits the [Read tool](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference.md#read-tool-behavior)'s token limit, 25,000 tokens by default. A text file larger than 256KB isn't included.

**2. Reference a directory**

```text wrap theme={null}
What's the structure of @src/components?
```

**3. Reference MCP resources**

```text wrap theme={null}
Show me the data from @github:repos/owner/repo/issues
```

This fetches data from connected MCP servers using the format @server:resource. See [MCP resources](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md#use-mcp-resources) for details.

> [!TIP]
>
> Tips:
>
> * File paths can be relative or absolute
> * Type `@` to open a path suggestion menu, then press Enter or Tab to accept the highlighted path and Enter again to send the message
> * @ file references add `CLAUDE.md` in the file's directory and parent directories to context
> * Directory references show file listings, not contents
> * You can reference multiple files in a single message (for example, "@file1.js and @file2.js")

To stop `@` references from including file contents and directory listings, set [`CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FILE_MENTIONS`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars#variables) to `1` in your shell or in the [`env` block](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars#set-variables-in-settings-files) of user settings or [managed settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings.md). Claude then receives the paths you referenced with a note to read them using its file tools. The variable requires Claude Code v2.1.299 or later, and Claude Code ignores it in project and local settings.

Your [`PreToolUse` hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#pretooluse) don't run when Claude Code includes a file you reference with `@`, because it makes no tool call. If you rely on those hooks to control what Claude reads, block specific paths or stop `@` references from including files:

* **Block specific paths**: add a [`Read` deny rule](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions#read-and-edit) for them. Claude Code doesn't include a file that the rule matches.
* **Stop `@` references from including files**: set `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FILE_MENTIONS=1`, which stops `@` file and directory references in your messages from including content, even for paths your hooks don't check. Your matching hooks then run before Claude opens a referenced path with a tool such as `Read`.

***

### Run Claude on a schedule

Suppose you want Claude to handle a task automatically on a recurring basis, like reviewing open PRs every morning, auditing dependencies weekly, or checking for CI failures overnight.

Pick a scheduling option based on where you want the task to run:

| Option | Where it runs | Best for |
| :- | :- | :- |
| [Cloud scheduled tasks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/routines.md) | Cloud, Anthropic-managed by default | Tasks that should run even when your computer is off. Can also trigger on API calls or GitHub events in addition to a schedule. Configure at [claude.ai/code/routines](https://claude.ai/code/routines). |
| [Desktop scheduled tasks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop-scheduled-tasks.md) | Your machine, via the desktop app | Tasks that need direct access to local files, tools, or uncommitted changes. |
| [GitHub Actions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/github-actions.md) | Your CI pipeline | Tasks tied to repo events like opened PRs, or cron schedules that should live alongside your workflow config. |
| [`/loop`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/scheduled-tasks) | The current CLI session | Quick polling while a session is open. `--resume` and `--continue` restore unexpired fixed-interval loops. |

> [!TIP]
>
> When writing prompts for scheduled tasks, be explicit about what success looks like and what to do with results. The task runs autonomously, so it can't ask clarifying questions. For example: "Review open PRs labeled `needs-review`, leave inline comments on any issues, and post a summary in the `#eng-reviews` Slack channel."

***

### Ask Claude about its capabilities

Claude can answer questions about its own features and limitations. It looks up the answers in the current Claude Code documentation, so they aren't limited to the version you're running.

#### Example questions

```text wrap theme={null}
can Claude Code create pull requests?
```

```text wrap theme={null}
how does Claude Code handle permissions?
```

```text wrap theme={null}
what skills are available?
```

```text wrap theme={null}
how do I use MCP with Claude Code?
```

```text wrap theme={null}
how do I configure Claude Code for Amazon Bedrock?
```

```text wrap theme={null}
what are the limitations of Claude Code?
```

> [!NOTE]
>
> Claude provides documentation-based answers to these questions. For hands-on demonstrations, run `/powerup` for interactive lessons with animated demos, or refer to the specific workflow sections above.

> [!TIP]
>
> Tips:
>
> * Ask specific questions to get detailed answers
> * Claude can explain complex features like MCP integration, enterprise configurations, and advanced workflows

***

## Resume previous conversations

When a task spans multiple sittings, pick up where you left off instead of re-explaining context. Claude Code saves every conversation locally.

```bash theme={null}
claude --continue
```

This resumes the most recent session in the current directory; if there isn't one yet, it prints `No conversation found to continue` and exits. Use `claude --resume` to choose from a list, or `/resume` from inside a running session. See [Manage sessions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions.md) for naming, branching, and the full picker reference.

## Run parallel sessions with worktrees

Work on a feature in one terminal while Claude fixes a bug in another, without the edits colliding. Each [git worktree](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree) is a separate checkout on its own branch, created from an existing commit, so the repository needs at least one commit first.

```bash theme={null}
claude --worktree feature-auth
```

Run the same command with a different name in a second terminal to start an isolated parallel session. See [Worktrees](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/worktrees.md) for cleanup, `.worktreeinclude`, and non-git VCS support. To monitor parallel sessions from one screen instead of separate terminals, see [background agents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-view.md).

## Plan before editing

For changes you want to review before they touch disk, switch to plan mode. Claude reads files and proposes a plan but makes no edits until you approve. The status bar shows `⏸ plan mode on` while plan mode is active.

```bash theme={null}
claude --permission-mode plan
```

You can also press `Shift+Tab` mid-session until the status bar shows `⏸ plan mode on`. See [Plan mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md#analyze-before-you-edit-with-plan-mode) for the approval flow and editing the plan in your text editor.

## Delegate research to subagents

Exploring a large codebase fills your context with file reads. Delegate the exploration so only the findings come back.

```text wrap theme={null}
use a subagent to investigate how our auth system handles token refresh
```

The subagent reads files in its own context window and reports a summary. See [Subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md) for defining custom agents with their own tools and prompts.

## Pipe Claude into scripts

Run Claude non-interactively for CI, pre-commit hooks, or batch processing. Stdin and stdout work like any Unix tool.

```bash theme={null}
git log --oneline -20 | claude -p "summarize these recent commits"
```

See [Non-interactive mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/headless.md) for output formats, permission flags, and fan-out patterns.

## Next steps

> [card] [Best practices](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices.md)
>

>

>
> Run isolated parallel sessions

>

# How Claude remembers your project

> Give Claude persistent instructions with CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md files, and let Claude accumulate learnings automatically with auto memory.

Each Claude Code session begins with a fresh context window. Two mechanisms carry knowledge across sessions:

* **CLAUDE.md files**: instructions you write to give Claude persistent context. Claude can also read a repository's [`AGENTS.md` files](#agents-md) in place of CLAUDE.md
* **Auto memory**: notes Claude writes itself based on your corrections and preferences

This page covers how to:

* [Write and organize CLAUDE.md files](#claude-md-files)
* [Use an existing AGENTS.md](#agents-md) as your project instructions
* [Scope rules to specific file types](#organize-rules-with-claude/rules/) with `.claude/rules/`
* [Configure auto memory](#auto-memory) so Claude takes notes automatically
* [Troubleshoot](#troubleshoot-memory-issues) when instructions aren't being followed

## CLAUDE.md vs auto memory

Claude Code has two complementary memory systems. Both are loaded at the start of every conversation. Claude treats them as context, not enforced configuration. To block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a [PreToolUse hook](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide.md) instead. The more specific and concise your instructions, the more consistently Claude follows them.

| | CLAUDE.md files | Auto memory |
| :- | :- | :- |
| **Who writes it** | You | Claude |
| **What it contains** | Instructions and rules | Learnings and patterns |
| **Scope** | Project, user, or org | Per repository, shared across worktrees |
| **Loaded into** | Every session | Every session (first 200 lines or 25KB) |
...

## Where Claude Code finds skills

The documentation's location table lists each source, its path, and where it loads:

| Location | Path | Loads in |
| :- | :- | :- |
| Enterprise | `.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` in the [managed settings directory](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-settings.md#delivery-mechanisms) | All users on machines where your organization deploys it |
| Personal | `~/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` | "All your projects on this machine, but not Cowork or cloud sessions" |
| Project | `.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` | "Sessions in this repository, but not cloud threads in a project. Commit it so your team gets it too" |
| Nested | `<subdir>/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` | "Sessions started in or below `<subdir>`, but not cloud threads in a project. Outside those threads, a session started above it loads the skill once Claude works on files there" |
| Additional directory | `.claude/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` in a directory you pass with `--add-dir` | "That session" |
| Plugin | `<plugin>/skills/<skill-name>/SKILL.md` | "Wherever the plugin is enabled, as `/plugin-name:skill-name`" |

Enterprise is the managed settings path, for example `/etc/claude-code/.claude/skills/<skill-name>/` on Linux.

## Precedence

When names collide, the docs say: "Enterprise over personal, and personal over project. With `deploy` in both `~/.claude/skills/` and the project's `.claude/skills/`, `/deploy` runs the personal one." Plugin skills don't collide with these, because they are namespaced: "Both load, because plugin skills are namespaced as `/plugin-name:skill-name`."

## Monorepos and nested directories

- **Parent directories:** "Claude Code loads project skills from `.claude/skills/` in the directory where you start it and in every parent directory up to the repository root, so starting in `packages/frontend/` still picks up skills defined at the root."
- **Worktrees:** In a linked git worktree, "Claude Code searches parent directories only up to the worktree root. On Claude Code v2.1.277 or later, when the worktree checkout has no `.claude/skills` directory at its root, Claude Code loads the main checkout's project skills instead."
- **Subdirectories load lazily:** "Skills in a `.claude/skills/` directory below where you started don't load at startup. They load the first time Claude reads or edits a file in that subdirectory and stay available for the rest of the session." To load them sooner, run `/add-dir` with the subdirectory path (v2.1.257 or later).
- **Moving with `/cd`:** On v2.1.246 or later, "Claude Code adds the new directory's project skills."
- **Same-named nested skills:** With a root `deploy` skill and `apps/web/.claude/skills/deploy/`, "`/deploy` runs the root skill" and "`/apps/web:deploy` runs the nested skill on its own."

## Directories added with `--add-dir`

"When you add a directory with `--add-dir` or `/add-dir`, Claude Code loads the skills in that directory's `.claude/skills/`, along with its `.claude/commands/` and `.claude/agents/`." Directories added through the Agent SDK's `additionalDirectories` or `add_dirs` load the same way. However, "The `permissions.additionalDirectories` setting in `settings.json` grants file access only and loads none of these."

- **Watching:** Only `.claude/skills/` is watched for changes. "It doesn't watch the added directory's `.claude/commands/` or `.claude/agents/`, so restart the session after changing a file there."
- **Prefixing on conflicts:** "An added directory's skill gets a prefix when its folder name clashes with an enterprise, personal, or project skill, or one in a directory added earlier." Example: with `--add-dir ../cli` and a `verify` skill in both your project and `../cli`, "`/verify` runs your project's skill" and "`/cli:verify` runs the skill from `../cli`." This requires v2.1.309 or later.
- **Restrictions:** Loading depends on the `project` setting source, which is on by default. A `strictPluginOnlyCustomization` policy, bare mode, and `--safe-mode` each restrict it further.

## Other discovery behavior

- **Live changes:** "When you add, edit, or remove a skill under `~/.claude/skills/`, the project `.claude/skills/`, or a `.claude/skills/` inside an `--add-dir` directory, Claude Code picks up the change within the current session, without a restart." If you create a new top-level skills directory, run `/reload-skills`.
- **Symlinks:** A skill folder in the enterprise, personal, or project location "can be a symlink to a directory elsewhere on disk," and Claude Code "loads the skill once even if several locations point at the same target."
- **Cowork and cloud sessions** don't read `~/.claude/skills/`. Those sessions load skills enabled for your claude.ai account instead.

def find_root(explicit: str | None) -> Path:
    if explicit:
        root = Path(explicit).resolve()
        if not (root / ".gitmodules").exists():
            raise UsageError(f"{root} has no .gitmodules")
        return root
    cwd = Path.cwd()
    for cand in (
        git("rev-parse", "--show-superproject-working-tree", cwd=cwd, check=False),
        git("rev-parse", "--show-toplevel", cwd=cwd, check=False),
    ):
        if cand and (Path(cand) / ".gitmodules").exists():
            return Path(cand).resolve()
    # Inside a child worktree under .worktrees/: walk up to the superproject.
    for base in [cwd, *cwd.parents]:
        if (base / ".gitmodules").exists() and (base / ".git").exists():
            return base.resolve()
    raise UsageError("not inside a superproject (no .gitmodules found); pass --root")

def wt_path(root: Path, s: Sub, branch: str) -> Path:
    return root / WORKTREE_DIR / s.path / branch.replace("/", "-")


def ensure_gitignore(root: Path, dry_run: bool) -> bool:
    """Return True when .gitignore needs (or got) the .worktrees/ entry."""
    if git_rc("check-ignore", "-q", "--no-index", f"{WORKTREE_DIR}/probe", cwd=root) == 0:
        return False
    if not dry_run:
        gi = root / ".gitignore"
        text = gi.read_text() if gi.exists() else ""
        sep = "" if not text or text.endswith("\n") else "\n"
        gi.write_text(f"{text}{sep}# superproject-workspace: child worktrees\n{WORKTREE_DIR}/\n")
    return True


def cmd_worktree(root: Path, subs: list[Sub], args) -> int:
    if args.wt_cmd == "list":
        chosen = [s for s in subs if is_initialized(root, s)]
        items = [dict(wt, submodule=s.name) for s in chosen for wt in list_child_worktrees(root, s)]
        rows = [["SUBMODULE", "BRANCH", "PATH", "STATE"]]
        for wt in items:
            state = ["prunable"] if wt["prunable"] else []
            if wt.get("dirty"):
                state.append(f"dirty({wt['dirty']})")
            if wt["merged"]:
                state.append("merged: safe to remove")
            rows.append([wt["submodule"], wt["branch"] or "(detached)", wt["path"], ", ".join(state)])
        emit(args, {"worktrees": items}, table(rows) if items else "no child worktrees")
        return 0

    s = resolve(subs, args.submodule)
    p = root / s.path
    if not is_initialized(root, s):
        raise Refused(f"{s.name} is not initialized; run `init {s.name}` first")
    target = wt_path(root, s, args.branch)
    rel = str(target.relative_to(root))

    if args.wt_cmd == "remove":
        cmd = ["worktree", "remove", *(["--force"] if args.force else []), str(target)]
        if not args.dry_run:
            git(*cmd, cwd=p)
            git("worktree", "prune", cwd=p)
            if args.delete_branch:
                git("branch", "-D" if args.force else "-d", args.branch, cwd=p)
        emit(args, {"removed": rel, "dry_run": args.dry_run}, f"{'would remove' if args.dry_run else 'removed'} {rel}")
        return 0

    # add
    if target.exists():
        raise Refused(f"{rel} already exists")
    if not args.no_fetch:
        fetch(p)
    branch = s.eff_branch(root)
    if ref_exists(p, f"refs/heads/{args.branch}"):
        cmd, base = ["worktree", "add", str(target), args.branch], args.branch
    elif ref_exists(p, f"refs/remotes/origin/{args.branch}"):
        base = f"origin/{args.branch}"
        cmd = ["worktree", "add", "--track", "-b", args.branch, str(target), base]
    else:
        # Pinned children branch from the recorded baseline, not from upstream tip.
        base = args.base or (f"origin/{branch}" if s.eff_policy == "track" else gitlink(root, s.path))
        cmd = ["worktree", "add", "-b", args.branch, str(target), base]
    gi = ensure_gitignore(root, args.dry_run)
    if not args.dry_run:
        target.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        git(*cmd, cwd=p)
    data = {"path": rel, "branch": args.branch, "base": base, "gitignore_updated": gi, "dry_run": args.dry_run}
    emit(args, data, f"{'would create' if args.dry_run else 'created'} {rel} on {args.branch} from {base}"

# Superproject orchestration only. All deploy recipes pin chezmoi to one of
# the sibling submodule checkouts; they never use chezmoi's default source.

set shell := ["sh", "-uc"]
set windows-shell := ["pwsh.exe", "-NoLogo", "-NoProfile", "-Command"]

root := justfile_directory()
unix_source := root / "dotfiles-unix"
windows_source := root / "dotfiles-windows"
ish_source := root / "dotfiles-iSH"
openwrt_source := root / "dotfiles-OpenWrt"
termux_source := root / "dotfiles-Termux"
unix_justfile := unix_source / "justfile"
windows_justfile := windows_source / "justfile"
native_source := if os_family() == "windows" { windows_source } else { unix_source }
native_init := if os_family() == "windows" { "--init" } else { "" }

# List the superproject recipes.
default:
    @just --list

# Apply the checkout matching this host (macOS/Linux/WSL -> Unix; Windows -> Windows).
apply *ARGS: _native-guard
    chezmoi apply --source="{{ native_source }}" {{ native_init }} {{ ARGS }}

# Explicitly apply the Unix checkout; unavailable on native Windows.
[unix]
apply-unix *ARGS: _native-guard
    chezmoi apply --source="{{ unix_source }}" {{ ARGS }}

# Explicitly apply the Windows checkout; unavailable off native Windows.
[windows]
apply-windows *ARGS:
    chezmoi apply --source="{{ windows_source }}" --init {{ ARGS }}

# Diff the checkout matching this host without opening a pager.
diff *ARGS: _native-guard
    chezmoi diff --source="{{ native_source }}" --no-pager {{ ARGS }}

# Show chezmoi status for the checkout matching this host.
status *ARGS: _native-guard
    chezmoi status --source="{{ native_source }}" {{ ARGS }}

# Preview a native apply verbosely without changing the destination.
dry-run *ARGS: _native-guard
    chezmoi apply --source="{{ native_source }}" {{ native_init }} --dry-run --verbose --no-pager {{ ARGS }}

# Run the validation suite appropriate for this host.
[unix]
check: check-unix

# Run the validation suite appropriate for this host.
[windows]
check: check-windows

# Validate the Unix checkout: lint, Bats, then source-pinned chezmoi dry-run.
[unix]
check-unix: _native-guard
    just --justfile "{{ unix_justfile }}" --working-directory "{{ unix_source }}" lint
    just --justfile "{{ unix_justfile }}" --working-directory "{{ unix_source }}" bats
    chezmoi apply --source="{{ unix_source }}" --dry-run --verbose --no-pager

# Validate Windows code without deploying it (also usable from macOS/Linux with pwsh + uv).
check-windows:
    just --justfile "{{ windows_justfile }}" --working-directory "{{ windows_source }}" lint
    just --justfile "{{ windows_justfile }}" --working-directory "{{ windows_source }}" test
    just --justfile "{{ windows_justfile }}" --working-directory "{{ windows_source }}" docs-build

# Show outer, gitlink, and all inner worktree states.
submodule-status:
    @echo "== superproject =="
    git status --short --branch
    @echo "== gitlinks =="
    git submodule status --recursive
    @echo "== dotfiles-unix =="
    git -C "{{ unix_source }}" status --short --branch
    @echo "== dotfiles-windows =="
    git -C "{{ windows_source }}" status --short --branch
    @echo "== dotfiles-iSH =="
    git -C "{{ ish_source }}" status --short --branch
    @echo "== dotfiles-OpenWrt =="
    git -C "{{ openwrt_source }}" status --short --branch
    @echo "== dotfiles-Termux =="
    git -C "{{ termux_source }}" status --short --branch

# Show unstaged and staged gitlink changes with commit logs.

    @echo "== staged gitlinks =="
    git diff --cached --submodule=log -- dotfiles dotfiles-unix dotfiles-windows dotfiles-iSH dotfiles-OpenWrt dotfiles-Termux

# Fetch and prune all submodule remotes without moving either checkout.
submodule-fetch:
    git -C "{{ unix_source }}" fetch --prune origin
    git -C "{{ windows_source }}" fetch --prune origin
    git -C "{{ ish_source }}" fetch --prune origin
    git -C "{{ openwrt_source }}" fetch --prune origin
    git -C "{{ termux_source }}" fetch --prune origin

# Synchronize local submodule URLs from .gitmodules.
submodule-sync:
    git submodule sync --recursive

# Initialize/update submodules to the commits recorded by the superproject.
submodule-bootstrap: submodule-sync
    git submodule update --init --recursive

# Switch all submodules to main and fast-forward them from origin/main.
[script("bash", "-eu", "-o", "pipefail")]
[unix]

    repos=(dotfiles-unix dotfiles-windows dotfiles-iSH dotfiles-OpenWrt dotfiles-Termux)
    for repo in "${repos[@]}"; do
        expected="$(cd "$repo" && pwd -P)"
        actual="$(git -C "$repo" rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null || true)"
        if [[ "$actual" != "$expected" ]]; then
            echo "error: $repo is not initialized; run: just submodule-bootstrap" >&2
            exit 1
        fi
        dirty="$(git -C "$repo" status --porcelain --untracked-files=all)"

            git -C "$repo" merge-base --is-ancestor origin/main main || remote_behind=$?

                echo "error: $repo main has diverged from origin/main; resolve it manually" >&2
                exit 1

            git -C "$repo" switch main
        else
            git -C "$repo" switch --track -c main origin/main
        fi
        git -C "$repo" merge --ff-only origin/main
    done
    git submodule status --recursive

        if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { $recordedSha = "" } else { $recordedSha = $recordedSha.Trim() }
        if ($indexSha -eq $recordedSha) { continue }
        $changed = $true

        $actual = git -C $repo rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>$null
        if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0 -or [System.IO.Path]::GetFullPath($actual.Trim()) -ne $expected) {

    python3 {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts/init_submodules.py") }} personal "$@"

# Opt into references, optionally selecting one owner/name; do not recurse.
submodules-references *args:
    python3 {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts/init_submodules.py") }} references "$@"

submodules-test:
    python3 -m unittest discover -s {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts") }} -p test_init_submodules.py -v

# Manage optional controller tunnels; setup is separate from starting visitors.
frp *args:
    @uv run --no-config --locked --script {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts/frp.py") }} "$@"

frp-setup *args:
    @just --justfile {{ quote(justfile()) }} frp setup "$@"

frp-up:
    @just --justfile {{ quote(justfile()) }} frp up

frp-down:
    @just --justfile {{ quote(justfile()) }} frp down

frp-status:
    @just --justfile {{ quote(justfile()) }} frp status

frp-health:
    @just --justfile {{ quote(justfile()) }} frp health

frp-test:
    @PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 uv run --no-config --with psutil==7.0.0 python {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts/test_frp.py") }}

# Private, offline formula/model comparison against explicitly selected sources.
feature-parity *args:
    @uv run --no-config --locked --script {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts/feature_parity.py") }} "$@"

# Install the checkout-local operations CLI; no Rust build or global installation.
ops-setup:
    UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT={{ quote(ops_venv) }} uv sync --locked --directory {{ quote(devops) }} --python 3.12

# Forward to the original CLI (including mutating commands); relative paths use devops/.
tarlino *args: _ops-ready
    @UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT={{ quote(ops_venv) }} uv run --no-sync --directory {{ quote(devops) }} -- {{ quote(ops_venv / "bin/tarlino") }} "$@"

# Read basic HX installation/service status; not a complete health check.
hx-status:
    @just --justfile {{ quote(justfile()) }} tarlino host status --variant hx --limit hx-ops

# Install a specific GitHub release and select it for subsequent starts. No restart.
[confirm("Change production bin/lib links on hx-ops? No restart, but the next scheduled start will use this version.")]
hx-deploy version: (_version version)
    @just --justfile {{ quote(justfile()) }} tarlino bin deploy --variant hx --limit hx-ops --version "$1"

# Select an already-installed release (also used for rollback). No restart.
[confirm("Switch production bin/lib links on hx-ops? No restart, but the next scheduled start will use this version.")]
hx-activate version: (_version version)
    @just --justfile {{ quote(justfile()) }} tarlino bin active --variant hx --limit hx-ops --version "$1"

# Build release binaries on a provisioned Linux x86_64 builder, without packaging.
tarlin-build variant: (_variant variant) _linux-x86_64
    make -C {{ quote(tarlin) }} build "VARIANT=$1" RELEASE=1

# Build the diagnostic CLI on the persistent Linux builder; optional target staging.
tarlint-build variant="hx" *args: (_variant variant)
    python3 {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts/remote_test_build.py") }} --variant "$1" "${@:2}"

# Build and package locally on Linux x86_64; never bump versions or publish.
tarlin-package variant: (_variant variant) _linux-x86_64
    env -u TARLIN_ARTIFACT_STORE make -C {{ quote(tarlin) }} release "VARIANTS=$1" BUMP=none STORE= ALLOW_DIRTY= CONTAINER=

[private]
_no-legacy-model:
    @test ! -e {{ quote(legacy_model) }} && test ! -L {{ quote(legacy_model) }} || { \
        printf '%s\n' 'Legacy submodules/conbond-deep-model checkout remains. Preserve any work outside that path, remove the legacy checkout, then rerun `just submodules`.' >&2; \
        exit 1; \
    }

[private]
_ops-ready:
    @test -x {{ quote(ops_venv / "bin/tarlino") }} && test -x {{ quote(ops_venv / "bin/ansible-playbook") }} || { printf '%s\n' 'Operations environment missing. Run: just ops-setup' >&2; exit 1; }

[private]
_version version:
    @[[ "$1" =~ ^v?[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+(-[0-9A-Za-z.-]+)?(\+[0-9A-Za-z.-]+)?$ ]] || { printf '%s\n' 'Provide an explicit version tag, e.g. v0.2.5 (not latest or a branch).' >&2; exit 1; }

[private]
_variant variant:
    @case "$1" in hx|gs) ;; *) printf '%s\n' 'Variant must be hx or gs.' >&2; exit 1 ;; esac

[private]
_linux-x86_64:
    @test "$(uname -s)" = Linux && test "$(uname -m)" = x86_64 || { printf '%s\n' 'Tarlin build/package requires a provisioned Linux x86_64 builder. This host can use ops-setup and deploy existing releases; CONTAINER=1 is not a complete macOS build/package route.' >&2; exit 1; }

sh010-status:

````text
     1	# Adopt superproject-workspace in existing superprojects
     2	
     3	**Status**: P2 (follow-up to #33)
     4	**Effort**: M per superproject
     5	**Related**: [`skills/local/superproject-workspace`](../skills/local/superproject-workspace/SKILL.md) · `references/case-patterns.md`
     6	
     7	## Context
     8	
     9	2026-10-28: `superproject-workspace` shipped with `audit` and `adopt`. A
    10	read-only smoke run against the maintainer's two reference superprojects (an
    11	umbrella and a workspace hub) found:
    12	
    13	- no policy keys
    14	- an umbrella child 9 commits ahead of its recorded pointer
    15	- several hub gitlinks reachable from no `origin` branch in local refs (re-check with `audit --fetch`)
    16	- checkouts sitting on feature branches with dirty trees
    17	- child paths hard-coded into duplicated sh/pwsh recipes
    18	
    19	The concrete per-repo checklists live in each superproject's own issue
    20	tracker, because those repos are private.
    21	
    22	## Generic adoption checklist
    23	
    24	1. `audit --fetch` and save the report. Resolve every `gitlink-unreachable`
    25	   error first by pushing the child commit or moving the pointer. A fresh
    26	   clone fails on these.
    27	2. Agree policies with the owner:
    28	   - children the outer repo should follow → `track`
    29	   - deployed or known-good baselines → `pin`, with `branch` set to the
    30	     baseline line
    31	   - references and rarely used children → `lazy`
    32	3. `adopt --dry-run --policy-default pin --set <child>=track:pr ...`, review,
    33	   then `adopt` (`--with-ci` once a `SUBMODULE_TOKEN` exists for private
    34	   children). Install the skill globally first (`npx skills add ...`), because
    35	   the recipes reference it instead of copying the CLI.
    36	4. Replace hand-written submodule recipes with the `sub-*` block. Keep
    37	   repo-specific recipes (deploy, build), but make them read paths from the CLI
    38	   rather than hard-coding them.
    39	5. Retire bespoke init scripts that the policy keys and `init --tier` now cover.
    40	6. Move ongoing child feature work into `.worktrees/<child>/<branch>`, or
    41	   document why it is kept outside.
    42	7. Commit the adoption as one outer commit. Run `audit --strict` in the
    43	   superproject's CI.
     1	# superproject-workspace
     2	
     3	Keep a **git-submodule superproject** usable as one agent entry point across
     4	many repos, without letting it drift. Use it for an umbrella of parallel repos,
     5	or for a workspace hub that mixes core, personal, and reference repos.
     6	
     7	A gitlink records a commit, not a branch, so drift is the default: child PRs
     8	merge and the pointer silently falls behind, checkouts end up detached or
     9	dirty, and pointers reference commits nobody pushed. The skill makes drift
    10	**visible** and moves pointers **by policy**.
    11	
    12	| Surface | Question it answers |
    13	|---|---|
    14	| `scripts/superproject.py status` | "Which children are behind, drifted, dirty, or pointing at unpushed commits?" |
    15	| `scripts/superproject.py pull` / `bump` | "How do I move pointers safely, all in one outer commit?" |
    16	| `scripts/superproject.py worktree` | "Where do I put a feature branch for a child?" |
    17	| `scripts/superproject.py audit` / `adopt` | "How do I bring an older superproject up to this standard?" |
    18	| `assets/superproject-bump.yml` | "How do pointers keep up without me remembering?" |
    19	| `references/decision-guide.md` | "Monorepo, submodules, manifest of clones, or Project add-dir?" |
    20	
    21	## Policy lives in `.gitmodules`
    22	
    23	```ini
    24	[submodule "app"]
    25	    path = app
    26	    url = git@github.com:me/app.git
    27	    branch = main
    28	    x-policy = track     # track | pin | lazy
    29	    x-bump = pr          # pr | direct | manual   (track only)
    30	    x-tier = core
    31	```
    32	
    33	| Policy | Pointer moves | Initialized |
    34	|---|---|---|
    35	| `track` | ff-only `pull`, then `bump`; optionally automated by CI (`pr` or `direct`) | by default |
    36	| `pin` | only `bump --reason` | by default |
    37	| `lazy` (`update = none`) | only `bump --reason` | only when named |
    38	
    39	## Core workflow
    40	
    41	```bash
    42	sp status --fetch
    43	sp worktree add app feat/login   # .worktrees/app/feat-login
    44	# ...commit + push + PR inside the child...
    45	sp pull
    46	sp bump --all-track --commit     # preflighted, one outer commit
    47	```
    48	
    49	To adopt an existing superproject, run
    50	`audit`, then `adopt --dry-run --policy-default pin --set app=track:pr`. After
    51	review, run `adopt`. It writes an AGENTS.md block, `sub-*` justfile recipes,
    52	the `.worktrees/` ignore entry, local git config, and, optionally, the CI
    53	workflow and pre-commit hook.
    54	
    55	The CLI is **referenced, not copied**: recipes resolve the installed skill
    56	(`~/.agents/skills/superproject-workspace`) and fall back to GitHub raw at
    57	`$SUPERPROJECT_CLI_REF`. One `npx skills update` upgrades every superproject.
    58	Rerun `adopt` to refresh the managed blocks; `audit` flags them when stale.
    59	
    60	(`sp` = `uv run --script ~/.agents/skills/superproject-workspace/scripts/superproject.py`, or the `just sub-*` recipes.)
    61	
    62	## See also
    63	
    64	- [Source](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/agent-skills/tree/main/skills/local/superproject-workspace)
    65	- [`git-workflow`](git-workflow.md): single-repo commits, branches, and worktrees.
    66	- [`forge-native-dev`](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/agent-skills/tree/main/skills/local/forge-native-dev): issue and PR lifecycle inside each child.

name: Superproject orchestration
on: [push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  check:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.12'
      - run: python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
#!/bin/sh
# Root recipes deliberately deploy only the desktop Unix/Windows repositories.
set -eu
if test -d /proc/ish || test -f /etc/openwrt_release; then
    echo 'Use the standalone iSH/OpenWrt bootstrap; full Unix apply is unavailable here.' >&2
    exit 1
fi
android=false
case "${PREFIX:-}" in /data/data/com.termux/*|/data/user/0/com.termux/*) android=true ;; esac
if command -v getprop >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    sdk=$(getprop ro.build.version.sdk 2>/dev/null || true)
    case "$sdk" in ''|*[!0-9]*) ;; *) android=true ;; esac
fi
if test "$android" = true; then
    echo 'Use dotfiles-Termux/bootstrap.sh inside Termux; adb shell and Android must not receive the desktop Unix configuration.' >&2
    exit 1
fi
# dotfiles-all

Five independent repositories, checked out together for maintenance.

| Directory | Upstream | Support |
|---|---|---|
| `dotfiles-unix/` | [dotfiles](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles) | Primary: macOS/Linux/WSL |
| `dotfiles-windows/` | [dotfiles-windows](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles-windows) | Secondary: native Windows |
| `dotfiles-iSH/` | [dotfiles-iSH](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles-iSH) | Experimental: minimal iSH |
| `dotfiles-OpenWrt/` | [dotfiles-OpenWrt](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles-OpenWrt) | Experimental: minimal OpenWrt/ImmortalWrt, Pi first |
| `dotfiles-Termux/` | [dotfiles-Termux](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles-Termux) | Experimental: Android native Bash/pkg, ADB-to-SSH setup |

```sh
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles-all.git
just submodule-status
just check-superproject
```

The Unix folder was renamed locally; its GitHub repository remains `dotfiles`.
The active chezmoi clone on this Mac is a separate checkout. Root apply/diff pin
the selected submodule source. iSH/OpenWrt/Termux use their own native bootstrap scripts.

Read [platform support](docs/platform-support.md), [orchestration](docs/superproject-justfile.md),
and the [cross-platform notes](docs/README.md). Commit/push affected inner repos
before one outer gitlink commit. Never rewrite unrelated staged work.

Android setup from macOS/Linux: `just termux-host-deps --install`, then
`just termux-devices` and `just termux-setup`. Use `just termux-ssh` to reconnect
and `just check-termux` for desktop validation. See the
[Termux setup guide](https://github.com/daviddwlee84/dotfiles-Termux/blob/main/docs/setup.md)
for device authorization, native installation, and manual fallback.

```text
set dotenv-load := true

# list recipes
default:
    @just --list

# first-time setup: init writable libs/ and knowledge/ submodules (never references/) and install deps
setup:
    git submodule update --init libs/alpha-risk-kit libs/quant-data-kit libs/featurelab knowledge/quant-factor-dictionary
    uv sync

# shallow-init read-only references: just refs <platforms|factors|factor-mining|models|evaluation|portfolio|data|learning|legacy|all>
refs category="all":
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    if [ "{{ category }}" = all ]; then prefix=references/; else prefix="references/{{ category }}/"; fi
    paths=$(git config -f .gitmodules --get-regexp '^submodule\..*\.path$' | awk '{print $2}' | grep "^$prefix" || true)
    [ -n "$paths" ] || { echo "no submodules under $prefix" >&2; exit 1; }
    for p in $paths; do
        echo "== $p"
        git -c "submodule.$p.update=checkout" submodule update --init --depth 1 -- "$p"
    done

# show which submodules are initialized (- = not initialized)
refs-status:
    git submodule status

# (re)apply read-only policy to every references/* entry in .gitmodules (run after adding one)
refs-config:
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    for name in $(git config -f .gitmodules --get-regexp '^submodule\..*\.path$' | awk '{print $2}' | grep '^references/'); do
        git config -f .gitmodules "submodule.$name.shallow" true
        git config -f .gitmodules "submodule.$name.update" none
        git config -f .gitmodules "submodule.$name.fetchRecurseSubmodules" false
    done
    echo "updated .gitmodules; review with: git diff .gitmodules"

# legacy AlphaBaseline nested submodules (Jingle mirrors on gitlab.com/jingle-archive)

# run one experiment: just run configs/alpha_baseline/lgbm_reg.yaml [--smoke] [--set k=v]

# run one config on Google Colab (docs/guides/colab.md): just colab configs/alpha_baseline/xgb_reg.yaml --session alpha --keep

# start the dictionary container in the background

    uv run --script scripts/preview.py up dictionary --directory knowledge/quant-factor-dictionary --preferred-port 8123 --port {{ quote(port) }} --host {{ quote(host) }}

# stop and remove only the Hub container
docs-down:
    uv run --script scripts/preview.py down hub

# stop and remove only the dictionary container
dict-down:
    uv run --script scripts/preview.py down dictionary

# follow Hub container logs (Ctrl+C exits logs without stopping the server)
docs-logs:
    uv run --script scripts/preview.py logs hub

# follow dictionary container logs
dict-logs:
    uv run --script scripts/preview.py logs dictionary

# regression tests for preview port selection and container lifecycle
preview-test:
    uv run --script scripts/tests/test_preview.py

docs-build:
    uv run mkdocs build --strict

# open a marimo notebook: just nb notebooks/foo.py
nb path:
    uv run marimo edit {{ path }}

# MLflow UI over the local tracking store
mlflow:
    uv run mlflow ui --backend-store-uri "${MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI:-sqlite:///mlruns.db}"

# isolated qlib benchmark environment (never imported by src/)
qlib-sync:
    cd experiments/qlib && uv sync

test:
    uv run pytest

lint:
    uv run ruff check .
    uv run ruff format --check .

fmt:
    uv run ruff check --fix .
    uv run ruff format .

=====TONS
set shell := ["bash", "-eu", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"]
set positional-arguments

# Show commands without contacting hosts or installing dependencies.
default:
    @just --justfile {{ quote(justfile()) }} --list

# Initialize only missing direct children; preserve existing branches and changes.
submodules:
    @python3 {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts/workspace.py") }} init

# Verify direct children match their recorded gitlinks and have no local changes.
workspace-check:
    @python3 {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts/workspace.py") }} check

# Read versioned context; never execute recorded commands or fetch source URLs.
context *args:
    @uv run --no-config --locked --script {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts/project_context.py") }} "$@"

context-test:
    @just --justfile {{ quote(justfile()) }} context validate
    @uv run --no-config --locked --script {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts/test_project_context.py") }}

workspace-test:
    @python3 {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts/test_workspace.py") }}

todo *args:
    @bash {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts/todo-kanban.sh") }} "$@" {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "TODO.md") }}

# Local validation only. First context use may fetch its locked Python dependency.
check: workspace-check workspace-test context-test data-test
    @just --justfile {{ quote(justfile()) }} todo --validate-only

# Bounded, read-only data inventory. See --help for local/SSH invocation.
data-inventory *args:
    @python3 {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts/data_inventory.py") }} inventory "$@"

# Verify only the registered duplicate candidate scope; never deletes.
data-check-duplicates *args:
    @python3 {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts/data_inventory.py") }} duplicates "$@"

# Explicit cleanup from a verified report; revalidates protected paths and content.
data-cleanup *args:
    @python3 {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts/data_inventory.py") }} cleanup "$@"

data-test:
    @python3 {{ quote(justfile_directory() / "scripts/test_data_inventory.py") }}

 `/Users/zhouhanru/.claude/projects/-Users-zhouhanru-Documents-David-Program-agent-skills/9864ce10-101f-4de2-b084-621ae78459a0/tool-results/toolu_01WYTLpHpsPnWMBfM1gYjgA1.txt`

```text
1	> ## Documentation Index
2	> Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt
3	> Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
4	
5	# Let Claude coordinate ongoing work with Projects
6	
7	> Hand Claude a stream of related tasks in one conversation and let it run them as parallel cloud sessions that share repositories, instructions, and memory.
8	
9	> [!NOTE]
10	>
11	> Projects are in public beta on Pro, Max, and Ultra plans and rolling out gradually. The rollout started with accounts that have used [cloud sessions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web.md) and don't have existing projects in claude.ai chat or Cowork. Projects aren't offered on Team or Enterprise plans yet.
12	>
13	> If you don't see **Projects** in the sidebar at [claude.ai/code](https://claude.ai/code) or in the Code tab of the [desktop app](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop.md), check under **More** there. If it's missing there too, the rollout hasn't reached your account yet. You can [join the waitlist](https://claude.com/form/projects), and see [Run agents in parallel](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agents.md) for what you can use in the meantime.
14	
15	A project is one ongoing conversation where Claude coordinates a stream of related work for you. You tell it what needs doing and it starts a thread for each task.
16	
17	Each thread is usually a [cloud session](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web.md): Claude Code running in the cloud rather than on your machine. When a task needs something only your computer has, you can ask Claude to [run that thread on your computer](#run-a-thread-on-your-own-computer) instead of in the cloud, through [Remote Control](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control.md). Threads run in parallel, and you can check on them and steer them from your phone. Cloud threads keep going after you close your laptop, while a thread on your computer runs only while that computer is awake.
18	
19	Without a project, running several sessions means doing the coordinating yourself: you decide what each one works on, repeat the same background at the start of each, and check back to see which finished or needs an answer. With a project, you instead:
20	
21	* **Send work to one place**: paste a bug report, a stack trace, or a list of tasks into the conversation whenever one comes up. Claude starts a thread for each piece of work or passes it to the thread already working in that area, and answers quick questions in place.
22	* **Set context once**: every new thread starts with the project's instructions, so a rule you state once, such as which branch to target, reaches all of them.
23	* **Walk away and come back to finished work**: the Overview pane shows which threads finished, which pull requests are ready for review, and which thread is waiting for your answer.
24	
25	If you already know the work you want a project to run, go straight to [Create a project](#create-a-project).
26	
27	## When to use a project
28	
29	A project is worth creating when the work has a goal that outlasts one session and keeps producing tasks. These kinds of work suit a project well:
30	
31	* **One goal across many repositories**: "Bring every service up to the new lint config." Claude can run a thread per repository, each with its own pull request, and the [Overview pane](#see-what-needs-you-in-overview) shows which ones are ready for review.
32	* **An area you keep feeding**: the bugs, stack traces, and review requests for one service, pasted into the conversation as they reach you. A pitfall you tell Claude to remember after one fix is in [project memory](#give-a-project-standing-context) for the next.
33	* **A build or migration bigger than a session**: "Build what `docs/spec.md` describes" or "Move the app off the deprecated ORM." The work splits into threads that each take a part, decisions you ask Claude to remember early on reach the later cloud threads, and the spec changes and bugs you find during the build go into the same conversation.
34	* **Work that isn't code**: a folder of contracts or a support-ticket export you keep coming back to with new questions, such as "find the ten most common integration mistakes in these tickets." Upload the documents instead of adding a repository, and threads deliver each write-up as a file in the project's [**Library**](#see-what-needs-you-in-overview).
35	
36	In any of them you can send a batch of tasks, tell Claude to start without asking you to confirm, and walk away. When you're back, you can find the threads that need you under [**Waiting on you**](#see-what-needs-you-in-overview). You can also ask Claude to put part of the work on a schedule as a [cloud scheduled task](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/routines.md). If one of these is your situation, [create a project](#create-a-project).
37	
38	### When something else fits better
39	
40	A project still fits when only some tasks need your machine. Cloud threads work on GitHub repositories and on the files, folders, and Google Drive folders you upload to the project, and for the occasional task that needs a local database or a tool on your computer, you can ask Claude to [run that task's thread on your computer](#run-a-thread-on-your-own-computer). Something other than a project fits better in these cases:
41	
42	* **One task that fits in a session**: "Fix the flaky login test." Start a [cloud session](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web.md) yourself.
43	* **Work where every task needs your machine**: a local database, a device emulator, or an API behind your VPN. Use a local session, or [agent view](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-view.md) to run several at once. If the work only needs local files, upload them to the project instead.
44	* **One task that repeats on a schedule with no conversation around it**: "Post a dependency report every Monday." Create a [cloud scheduled task](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/routines.md) on its own.
45	* **Several people giving Claude work and steering it together in a Slack channel**: see [Claude Tag](https://claude.com/docs/claude-tag/overview).
46	
47	A project draws on the same plan limits as your other Claude Code sessions and uses them faster. [Usage and cost](#usage-and-cost) covers what draws on your plan and how to keep it down.
48	
49	## How a project is organized
50	
51	A project is one coordinating conversation with Claude plus the threads it starts to do the work. These are its parts:
52	
53	* **The project conversation**: one long-running session where Claude acts as coordinator. It takes what you send, decides what becomes a thread, and keeps track of every thread it started. It sees what threads report back, not every step they take.
54	* **Threads**: the workers. Each is a separate session with its own context window that does one piece of work and reports back to the conversation when it finishes. A cloud thread works on its own branch and opens a pull request when the work calls for one.
55	* **What every cloud thread starts with**:
56	  * The project's repositories and files, plus its [instructions and memory](#give-a-project-standing-context)
57	  * The `CLAUDE.md` in [each of the project's repositories](#what-threads-pick-up-from-your-repositories), but not the repositories' skills, `.claude/settings.json`, or `.mcp.json`
58	  * The [connectors](#get-skills-plugins-connectors-and-tools-into-threads) on your claude.ai account
59	  * A [cloud environment](#choose-an-environment-for-threads) that sets its network access, environment variables, network secrets, and installed tools
60	* **The Overview pane**: where you [see all the threads at once](#see-what-needs-you-in-overview) and which of them need you.
61	
62	Cloud threads don't pick up anything from the Claude Code setup on your own machine. [Get skills, plugins, connectors, and tools into threads](#get-skills-plugins-connectors-and-tools-into-threads) covers how to give them what they'd otherwise be missing.
63	
64	Here is how those parts connect, from you through the conversation to the threads doing the work, with Overview tracking their state:
65	
66	![Diagram of a project. You write in the project conversation, where Claude answers or starts a thread. Each cloud thread works on its own branch and pull request. The Overview pane lists threads by state, such as ready for review, waiting on you, and working.](https://mintcdn.com/claude-code/e8CLbxM17eD7cAiv/images/claude-projects-overview.svg?fit=max\&auto=format\&n=e8CLbxM17eD7cAiv\&q=85\&s=dbf446f69f0bbdb9961d21af207cb93b)
67	
68	## Create a project
69	
70	You create and use projects at [claude.ai/code](https://claude.ai/code), in the Code tab of the desktop app, or in the Claude mobile app for [iOS](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/claude-by-anthropic/id6473753684) and [Android](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.anthropic.claude). In the browser and the desktop app there are two ways to start a project:
71	
72	* **From scratch**, when you know the stream of work you want Claude to run: open the **New project** dialog and name it. [Start a new project from scratch](#start-a-new-project-from-scratch) walks through the dialog.
73	* **From a cloud session that's already doing the work**: in that session's sidebar menu, choose **Continue in project**, then **Continue as new project**. Claude proposes the project's setup from what the session was doing. See [Start from an existing cloud session](#start-from-an-existing-cloud-session).
74	
75	Either way, [check the prerequisites](#check-the-prerequisites) first.
76	
77	### Check the prerequisites
78	
79	Before you create a project, check your plan, your GitHub setup, and what the work needs to reach:
80	
81	* **Plan**: you're on Pro, Max, or Ultra, and **Projects** shows in your sidebar, directly or under **More**. Select **Projects** and check that it offers **New project** or **Get started**.
82	* **GitHub, if the project will work on code**: your code is on github.com rather than GitHub Enterprise Server, GitLab, or Bitbucket, your connected GitHub account has push access to it, and the Claude GitHub App is installed on it. If you connected GitHub with [`/web-setup`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/web-quickstart#connect-from-your-terminal), that token lets your other cloud sessions reach a repository but isn't enough for a project's cloud threads, which need the Claude GitHub App. [Set up GitHub access](#set-up-github-access) has the steps.
83	* **Network access, secrets, and tools**: for cloud threads, these come from the project's [cloud environment](#choose-an-environment-for-threads). The default environment already reaches [common package registries](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cloud-environments.md#default-allowed-domains), so check this only if the work needs other domains, a secret, or a tool that isn't preinstalled. If the work needs an MCP server, check that it shows as connected in your [claude.ai connectors](https://claude.ai/customize/connectors).
84	
85	### Start a new project from scratch
86	
87	Starting a project from scratch means opening the **New project** dialog, naming the stream of work, and optionally giving it a goal and the repositories and files it works on. Only the name is required, so you can create the project first and fill in the rest as the work takes shape.
88	
89	**1. Open Projects**
90	
91	At [claude.ai/code](https://claude.ai/code) or in the Code tab of the desktop app, select **Projects** in the left sidebar, or under **More** there. In a browser you can also go straight to [claude.ai/code/projects/browse](https://claude.ai/code/projects/browse). Then select **New project**. If the button reads **Get started** instead, select it and first upgrade or archive the existing claude.ai projects it lists.
92	
93	**2. Fill in the New project dialog**
94	
95	Scope the project to one stream of work you'll keep adding to, such as everything it takes to keep one API under its latency target. [When to use a project](#when-to-use-a-project) has more examples. Then fill in the dialog's fields:
96	
97	* **Name**: how the project appears in the **Projects** list.
98	* **What do you want to work on?** (optional): one line that becomes the project's goal, such as "Hold p95 API latency under 200 ms". Claude in the conversation works toward it. Without a goal, Claude works from the tasks you send, and you can add a goal later in **Project settings > General**.
99	* **Context** (optional): the GitHub repositories this project works on, plus any files, folders, or Google Drive folders threads should read. Click **+** for each. Add the repositories most tasks need rather than every one the work might touch; [Decide which repositories to add](#decide-which-repositories-to-add) covers the choice, and you can add more later in **Project settings > Environment**.
100	
101	Standing rules for how threads should work go in [project instructions](#give-a-project-standing-context), which you set after the project exists.
102	
103	**3. Create the project**
104	
105	Click **Create project**. The project's conversation opens with a message box at the bottom, where you describe work for Claude.
106	
107	On your first project, Claude takes a turn of its own as soon as the project is created, unless you send a message first. That turn uses your plan. In it, Claude may:
108	
109	* Start one thread that explores the repository without changing anything and proposes next steps, if the project has a repository it can read.
110	* Post **Setup recommendations** drawn from your recent cloud sessions: repositories to add, scheduled tasks to create, and threads it could start. Every recommended repository and scheduled task starts switched on. Switch off the ones you don't want, then click **Update setup** to add the rest, or ignore the recommendations and describe work yourself.
111	
112	The project is now in the sidebar, and its conversation is open. [Your first batch](#your-first-batch) covers what to set up before you send it work.
113	
114	### Start from an existing session
115	
116	If a cloud session you started yourself is doing work that belongs in a project, open its sidebar menu and choose **Continue in project**, then pick from the submenu:
117	
118	* Choose **Continue as new project** to create a new project from the session. The project opens, and Claude reads the session and posts **Setup recommendations** in the project conversation for you to confirm. The original session stays in your session list. If it was in the middle of a turn it keeps running, so stop it yourself if you don't want both working at once.
119	* Choose one of your existing projects to bring the session's work into that project. That project opens, and a message sent on your behalf asks Claude to read the session and pick up where it left off. The original session stays in your session list, unchanged.
120	
121	A **Set up project** banner can also appear above a cloud session's message box. If you use it instead of **Continue as new project**, the result is the same, except that the session's running turn stops once the project opens.
122	
123	A session on your own machine gets the same sidebar menu at claude.ai/code once you connect it through [Remote Control](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control.md#start-a-remote-control-session). From a project, Claude can't read the transcript of a session that connected while [**Require trusted devices**](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control.md#trusted-devices) was on for your account. If that setting is off:
124	
125	1. If the session isn't connected yet, run `/remote-control` in it. If it connected while that setting was on, disconnect it and connect it again first.
126	2. In a browser, find the session's row in the sidebar at [claude.ai/code](https://claude.ai/code), open its menu, and pick from the same submenu.
127	
128	If **Require trusted devices** is on, or you don't use Remote Control, describe the work in the project conversation yourself. Or push the session's branch, add its repository to the project, and tell Claude the branch name.
129	
130	### Set up GitHub access
131	
132	Most GitHub setup happens once, not per project. You connect your GitHub account to Claude once, and the Claude GitHub App is installed once per repository, or once for a whole GitHub organization if you give it all repositories. You come back to these steps when you add a repository the Claude GitHub App doesn't cover yet or one in a GitHub organization that enforces SSO.
133	
134	**1. Connect your GitHub account**
135	
136	If you haven't used claude.ai/code before, your first visit walks you through connecting GitHub; see [Connect GitHub](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/web-quickstart.md#connect-github). Otherwise use one of the [GitHub authentication options](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web.md#github-authentication-options).
137	
138	**2. Install the Claude GitHub App on the project's repositories**
139	
140	Install the [Claude GitHub App](https://github.com/apps/claude) and grant it the repositories the project will use. On a repository owned by a GitHub organization, only an organization owner can complete the install; if you aren't one, GitHub sends the owner an install request and the project can't use the repository until they approve it.
141	
142	**3. Authorize SSO for organizations that enforce it**
143	
144	If a GitHub organization enforces SAML SSO, reconnect GitHub and authorize the Claude app for that organization. Until you do, that organization's private repositories don't appear in the **New project** dialog or **Project settings > Environment**.
145	
146	When one of these steps is incomplete, the **New project** dialog and the project page name the missing step and link to where you finish it. Finish the step there, then click **Check again** if the dialog offers it. If a repository is still missing from the list afterward, open the Claude GitHub App's installation on GitHub, at [github.com/settings/installations](https://github.com/settings/installations) for a personal account, and confirm the repository is listed under **Repository access**. For the error messages a thread or the project reports when access is still wrong, see [Repository access errors](#repository-access-errors).
147	
148	## Work in a project
149	
150	Give Claude work through the project conversation: tasks one at a time or several at once, plus updates and loose thoughts as they come up. Claude routes each message, and threads do the work and report back.
151	
152	### Your first batch
153	
154	Before you send a new project a batch of work, set it up so the first threads come back the way you want:
155	
156	1. [Write project instructions](#write-project-instructions): the brief every thread starts from, such as which branch to target, how a thread checks its work, and what needs your go-ahead.
157	2. Send one small piece of the real work, or start one of the threads Claude suggested if it offered any, and open the thread when it finishes to see how it reports back and what it did on its branch. If it assumed something wrong or couldn't reach what it needed, [Threads guessed or stalled instead of asking](#threads-guessed-or-stalled-instead-of-asking) covers where to fix that.
158	3. Check **Thread model** and **Thread effort** in **Project settings > General**. A new project runs every thread on Opus at high effort, which draws on your plan fastest; [Choose models and let Claude manage context](#choose-models-and-let-claude-manage-context) covers the alternatives.
159	4. Ask Claude to [propose threads before starting them and to run a few at a time](#tune-how-claude-runs-a-project), and drop those limits once a few threads come back the way you want.
160	
161	### Send work and read results
162	
163	Claude decides where each message you send in the conversation goes:
164	
165	* A quick question usually gets an answer in the conversation.
166	* New work goes to a new thread or to a thread already working in that area, and Claude tells you which. Each new thread shows up under your message as a card: a box with the thread's title and status, which you click to open the thread.
167	* Several unrelated tasks in one message become separate threads.
168	
169	If Claude routes something differently than you wanted, say so. [Tune how Claude runs a project](#tune-how-claude-runs-a-project) lists things you can tell it, such as reusing an existing thread for follow-ups or answering in place instead of starting a thread.
170	
171	A thread's full results stay in the thread, and you open its card in the conversation to read them. Files a thread produced are also in the project's [**Library**](#see-what-needs-you-in-overview).
172	
173	Sometimes Claude proposes threads instead of starting them, in a **Suggested threads** list. Click the arrow on a suggestion to start that thread. When several are listed, a button under the list starts all of them.
174	
175	### Review a thread's pull request
176	
177	When a cloud thread changes code, this is what it does unless you tell it otherwise:
178	
179	* **Branch**: works on a new branch, started from the repository's default branch.
180	* **Pull request**: opens one when you ask, and can open one on its own for a bug fix or another concrete change.
181	* **After it opens**: watches the pull request with [auto-fix](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-code-on-the-web.md#auto-fix-pull-requests) turned on, whether or not auto-fix is on for your other cloud sessions. It pushes fixes when CI fails, addresses review comments, and replies in the thread when checks pass and the pull request is ready for you.
182	
183	When a thread has pushed a branch or opened a pull request, its card in the conversation can show a button for the next step:
184	
185	* **Resolve conflicts**, **Fix CI**, **Address comments**, and **Merge it** send that instruction to the thread as a message from you, so you can prompt the thread yourself instead of waiting for it to react to the pull request.
186	* **Review PR** opens the pull request on GitHub.
187	* **Create PR** appears when an idle thread has pushed a branch but hasn't opened a pull request. Clicking it creates the pull request from that branch directly rather than sending the thread an instruction to open one.
188	
189	To change when threads open pull requests, for example only when you ask, or which branch they start from, say so in the task or in [project instructions](#write-project-instructions).
190	
191	### See what needs you in Overview
192	
193	The Overview pane beside the conversation tracks the project's threads. It's already open the first time you open a new project. To reopen it after you close it, click the **Threads** button in the project header. The button shows a dot when a thread is waiting on you.
194	
195	In the desktop app, a notification appears by default when Claude posts in the conversation, a thread hits an error, or a thread needs your input. None appears while you're viewing the project. To also get one each time a thread finishes a turn, or to turn them off for a project, choose **Notifications** in the project's sidebar menu. In a browser, check the dot on the **Threads** button.
196	
197	The pane's **Threads** view groups threads by state:
198	
199	| Group | What's in it |
200	| :- | :- |
```
